Toxicology Chapter 178

Atypical and Serotonergic Antidepressants

This chapter covers bupropion, trazodone, mirtazapine, SSRIs, SNRIs, and the emergency pattern that matters most: serotonin syndrome.

Board lens: bupropion = delayed seizures; venlafaxine = seizures/QRS-QT/cardiotoxicity; serotonin syndrome = clonus + hyperreflexia + serotonergic exposure.

Overview

Newer antidepressants are generally safer than TCAs, but overdose still causes seizures, dysrhythmias, hypotension, serotonergic toxicity, and delayed complications depending on agent and formulation.

SNRIsVenlafaxine is the exam favorite for seizures and cardiotoxicity.

Bupropion

Tintinalli Source Check

Clinical features and treatment

Must remember: seizures can be delayed, especially extended-release. Adult extended-release ingestion >450 mg needs prolonged monitoring.

Trazodone

Trazodone overdose is usually sedation plus hemodynamic/ECG monitoring issues. Watch for orthostatic hypotension and QT prolongation.

SSRIs

Tintinalli Source Check
Tintinalli Source Check

Clinical features

SNRIs

Venlafaxine deserves special respect: seizures, QRS/QT changes, rhabdomyolysis, hypotension, and delayed toxicity are the reasons patients may need prolonged observation.

Tintinalli Source Check

Serotonin Syndrome

Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis. The strongest bedside pattern is serotonergic exposure plus clonus, tremor, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, agitation, diaphoresis, hyperthermia.

Drug Dose Reference

ProblemTreatment ReferenceBoard Caution
SeizureIV benzodiazepines; phenobarbital if persistent per tox guidanceDo not use phenytoin as first-line for toxicologic seizures.
QRS wideningSodium bicarbonate boluses/infusion per protocolEspecially important for venlafaxine or mixed sodium-channel blocker exposure.
QT prolongation / torsadesMagnesium sulfate 2 g IV; correct K/Mg; pacing/isoproterenol if refractory per ACLS/toxCitalopram/escitalopram, trazodone, venlafaxine can matter.
Serotonin syndrome mildStop serotonergic agents, supportive care, benzodiazepinesLook for clonus/hyperreflexia.
Serotonin syndrome moderate/severeAggressive cooling, IV fluids, benzodiazepines, consider cyproheptadine via enteral route; intubation/paralysis for severe hyperthermiaAntipyretics do not fix muscle-generated hyperthermia.
Early large ingestionActivated charcoal if within ~1 hour and airway protectedWhole-bowel irrigation may be considered for very large venlafaxine extended-release ingestion.

Key Points

Bupropion = seizuresDelayed seizures are the core risk, especially extended-release.
Venlafaxine is not benignSeizures, QRS/QT changes, hypotension, rhabdomyolysis.
SSRIs usually saferBut citalopram/escitalopram can produce ECG abnormalities.
TrazodoneOrthostatic hypotension, QT prolongation, CNS depression, rare torsades.
Serotonin syndromeClonus and hyperreflexia separate it from anticholinergic toxicity.
NMS contrastSlower onset, bradyreflexia, lead-pipe rigidity.
TreatmentStop agents, benzodiazepines, cooling, supportive care; cyproheptadine for selected cases.
ECG mattersUse cardiac monitoring and repeat ECG for high-risk agents or symptoms.

Chapter Assessment

Which overdose is most associated with delayed-onset seizures and need for prolonged observation after extended-release ingestion?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Sertraline
Incorrect choice
SSRIs are usually lower lethality and seizures are uncommon except selected agents/coingestions.
B. Bupropion
Correct choice
Bupropion has prominent seizure risk; extended-release products can have delayed seizures.
C. Mirtazapine
Incorrect choice
Mirtazapine overdose is usually sedating and relatively benign.
D. Paroxetine
Incorrect choice
Paroxetine is an SSRI and not the classic delayed seizure agent.

A patient on sertraline plus dextromethorphan has agitation, diaphoresis, tremor, inducible clonus, and hyperreflexia. Most likely diagnosis?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Serotonin syndrome
Correct choice
Serotonergic exposure plus clonus/hyperreflexia and autonomic findings is serotonin syndrome.
B. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Incorrect choice
NMS has slower onset and lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia.
C. Anticholinergic toxicity
Incorrect choice
Anticholinergic toxicity has dry skin/mucosa and normal reflexes rather than clonus.
D. Opioid withdrawal
Incorrect choice
Withdrawal can cause autonomic symptoms but does not explain clonus/hyperreflexia.

Best first-line treatment for seizures from bupropion, SSRI, or SNRI overdose?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Phenytoin
Incorrect choice
Phenytoin is not first-line for toxicologic seizures.
B. IV benzodiazepines
Correct choice
Tintinalli tables emphasize IV benzodiazepines for seizure control.
C. Physostigmine
Incorrect choice
Physostigmine is for selected anticholinergic delirium, not serotonergic seizures.
D. Naloxone
Incorrect choice
Naloxone treats opioid respiratory depression, not antidepressant seizures.

Which feature best distinguishes serotonin syndrome from anticholinergic toxicity?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Dry mucous membranes
Incorrect choice
Dry mucosa favors anticholinergic toxicity.
B. Normal muscle tone
Incorrect choice
Normal tone/reflexes favors anticholinergic toxicity.
C. Hyperreflexia and clonus
Correct choice
Hyperreflexia, clonus, tremor, and myoclonus are key serotonin findings.
D. Urinary retention only
Incorrect choice
Urinary retention is nonspecific and common in anticholinergic states.

Which SSRI/SNRI overdose pattern needs special attention for QRS/QT effects and seizures?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Fluoxetine mild nausea only
Incorrect choice
Fluoxetine is generally lower risk in isolated overdose.
B. Venlafaxine large ingestion
Correct choice
Venlafaxine/SNRI overdose can produce seizures, QRS/QT changes, hypotension, and rhabdomyolysis.
C. Mirtazapine therapeutic dose
Incorrect choice
Therapeutic mirtazapine is not the overdose pattern being asked.
D. Trazodone with isolated priapism
Incorrect choice
Priapism is a trazodone adverse effect, but this option does not capture the high-risk overdose pattern.

Recommended early ED management for pure SSRI overdose includes which of the following?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Routine dialysis
Incorrect choice
Dialysis is not routine for SSRI overdose.
B. Cardiac monitoring/ECG and benzodiazepines for seizures
Correct choice
Tintinalli emphasizes IV access, cardiac rhythm monitor, ECG, charcoal if early, and benzodiazepines for seizures.
C. Immediate flumazenil
Incorrect choice
Flumazenil is unrelated and risky in mixed overdose.
D. Empiric sodium nitrite
Incorrect choice
Sodium nitrite is a cyanide antidote, not SSRI therapy.

Trazodone overdose most characteristically causes which cardiovascular problem?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Orthostatic hypotension and QT prolongation
Correct choice
Trazodone overdose often causes CNS depression plus orthostatic hypotension and QT prolongation.
B. Severe hypertension from norepinephrine release
Incorrect choice
That is not the typical trazodone profile.
C. Complete heart block in most cases
Incorrect choice
Heart block is not the common presentation.
D. Immediate refractory VF in all ingestions
Incorrect choice
This overstates risk; torsades is rare but possible.

Which medication list should make you most worried about serotonin syndrome?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Sertraline, tramadol, linezolid
Correct choice
SSRI plus serotonergic opioid and linezolid is a high-risk serotonergic combination.
B. Diphenhydramine only
Incorrect choice
Diphenhydramine is anticholinergic/sedating, not primarily serotonergic.
C. Warfarin and metoprolol
Incorrect choice
These are not serotonergic.
D. Acetaminophen and ibuprofen
Incorrect choice
These are analgesics without serotonin syndrome risk in usual use.

Core management of serotonin syndrome is best described as:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Continue serotonergic agents and observe
Incorrect choice
Stopping serotonergic agents is essential.
B. Stop offending agents, supportive care, benzodiazepines, cooling; consider cyproheptadine for moderate/severe cases
Correct choice
This matches standard ED management principles.
C. Give haloperidol as definitive antidote
Incorrect choice
Antipsychotics may worsen temperature/rigidity concerns and are not definitive.
D. Dialysis for all cases
Incorrect choice
Dialysis is not routine therapy for serotonin syndrome.

Which serotonin syndrome pattern is severe?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Mild agitation, tremor, mydriasis, temperature <40C
Incorrect choice
This is more consistent with mild serotonin syndrome.
B. Marked agitation, fever >40C, hyperreflexia, ocular clonus
Incorrect choice
This is moderate severity.
C. Hyperthermia >41.1C, delirium, marked rigidity, marked BP/HR swings
Correct choice
Tintinalli severity table describes this as severe.
D. Dry skin, ileus, normal reflexes
Incorrect choice
This points more toward anticholinergic toxicity.

After a large bupropion extended-release ingestion, which disposition plan is safest even if the patient looks well initially?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Discharge after 2 hours if asymptomatic
Incorrect choice
Early wellness is unreliable after extended-release bupropion.
B. Discharge once the first ECG is normal
Incorrect choice
A normal initial ECG does not eliminate delayed seizure risk.
C. Observe only until nausea improves
Incorrect choice
GI symptoms are not the key endpoint for bupropion toxicity.
D. Prolonged monitored observation because seizures may be delayed
Correct choice
Bupropion, especially sustained/extended-release products, can produce delayed seizures and dysrhythmias.

Which antidepressant overdose is classically associated with alpha-1 blockade causing hypotension and also may prolong the QT interval?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Fluoxetine
Incorrect choice
Fluoxetine is an SSRI; isolated overdose is usually less cardiotoxic.
B. Bupropion
Incorrect choice
Bupropion is known for seizures and conduction abnormalities, not alpha-1 blockade.
C. Trazodone
Correct choice
Trazodone can cause CNS depression, alpha-1-mediated hypotension, and QT prolongation.
D. Mirtazapine
Incorrect choice
Mirtazapine is usually sedating and comparatively benign in isolated overdose.

Which SSRI deserves extra ECG and seizure attention in overdose compared with most other SSRIs?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Sertraline
Incorrect choice
Sertraline overdose is usually mild unless there are coingestants or serotonin syndrome.
B. Citalopram or escitalopram
Correct choice
These agents are notable among SSRIs for QT prolongation and seizure risk in significant overdose.
C. Fluvoxamine only when taken with food
Incorrect choice
Food timing is not the classic high-risk discriminator.
D. Paroxetine only if pupils are large
Incorrect choice
Mydriasis can occur but does not identify the ECG-risk SSRI pair.

A venlafaxine overdose patient has tachycardia, hypertension, agitation, seizure, and QRS/QT abnormalities. What is the key teaching point?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Venlafaxine can be more dangerous than typical isolated SSRI overdose
Correct choice
Venlafaxine overdose is associated with seizures, serotonin toxicity, and cardiovascular toxicity.
B. Venlafaxine overdose is always asymptomatic
Incorrect choice
Significant ingestions can be severe.
C. Naloxone reverses venlafaxine cardiotoxicity
Incorrect choice
Naloxone is not a venlafaxine antidote.
D. QT changes exclude SNRI toxicity
Incorrect choice
QT/QRS abnormalities can occur in serious SNRI toxicity.

Which physical exam finding most strongly separates serotonin syndrome from anticholinergic poisoning?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Mydriasis
Incorrect choice
Both toxidromes may have dilated pupils.
B. Clonus and hyperreflexia
Correct choice
Neuromuscular excitation, especially clonus/hyperreflexia, is the major serotonin syndrome clue.
C. Dry mouth and urinary retention
Incorrect choice
These point toward anticholinergic toxicity.
D. Sinus tachycardia
Incorrect choice
Tachycardia is nonspecific.

Which pattern favors neuroleptic malignant syndrome rather than serotonin syndrome?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Onset within hours after adding linezolid to an SSRI
Incorrect choice
Rapid onset after serotonergic interaction favors serotonin syndrome.
B. Ocular clonus and lower-extremity hyperreflexia
Incorrect choice
Clonus and hyperreflexia favor serotonin syndrome.
C. Slower onset with lead-pipe rigidity and decreased reflexes
Correct choice
NMS typically evolves more slowly and has rigidity with reduced reflexes rather than clonus.
D. Diarrhea and tremor after serotonergic overdose
Incorrect choice
GI hyperactivity and tremor fit serotonin toxicity.

A serotonin syndrome patient has temperature 41.5C, severe rigidity, and rapidly worsening acidosis. What should be added to benzodiazepines and external cooling?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Antipyretics as definitive therapy
Incorrect choice
This is muscle-generated hyperthermia, not a hypothalamic fever.
B. Physical restraints until agitation stops
Incorrect choice
Restraints can worsen heat production and acidosis.
C. Phenytoin loading
Incorrect choice
Phenytoin is not the core therapy for severe serotonin toxicity.
D. Intubation, deep sedation, and neuromuscular paralysis
Correct choice
Severe hyperthermia from rigidity requires aggressive supportive care to stop muscle activity and cool rapidly.

Cyproheptadine is best described as:

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. An oral/enteral serotonin antagonist used as adjunctive therapy for serotonin syndrome
Correct choice
Cyproheptadine can be given orally or via tube after stabilization; supportive care remains central.
B. An IV antidote that replaces airway and cooling management
Incorrect choice
There is no IV form that replaces resuscitation and cooling.
C. A sodium-channel blocker used for bupropion seizures
Incorrect choice
It is serotonergic antagonism, not seizure prophylaxis for bupropion.
D. A paralytic that directly lowers temperature
Incorrect choice
Cyproheptadine is not a neuromuscular blocker.

Which ECG finding after atypical antidepressant overdose should push you toward sodium bicarbonate therapy and ICU-level monitoring?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Isolated sinus bradycardia with narrow QRS
Incorrect choice
This does not describe sodium-channel blockade toxicity.
B. Wide QRS with ventricular dysrhythmia or hemodynamic instability
Correct choice
A wide QRS with instability suggests sodium-channel blockade physiology; treat supportively and involve toxicology early.
C. Normal QTc in an asymptomatic patient
Incorrect choice
This does not require bicarbonate.
D. First-degree AV block only after a therapeutic dose
Incorrect choice
This isolated finding is not the typical trigger for bicarbonate therapy.

Which patient most clearly needs admission or extended observation after antidepressant overdose?

Why each choice is right or wrong
A. Adult with small isolated sertraline ingestion, normal ECG, and no symptoms after observation
Incorrect choice
This may be appropriate for discharge after poison-center guided observation.
B. Mild nausea only after a single low-dose mirtazapine ingestion
Incorrect choice
Mirtazapine is usually low risk in isolated small overdose.
C. Extended-release bupropion ingestion with tachycardia and tremor
Correct choice
Tachycardia/tremor after bupropion XR flags risk for delayed seizures and need for monitored observation.
D. Accidental double dose of fluoxetine with normal exam
Incorrect choice
This is usually low risk compared with symptomatic bupropion XR ingestion.
